title: Your Smartwatch May Not be as Smart as You Think it is - Nautilus
gist: Roughly 30-40% of American adults now own a smartwatch, but University of Michigan kinesiologists have published a new framework highlighting that the accuracy of the health metrics these devices report (blood pressure, sweat loss, etc.) is questionable.

insights.claim: An estimated 30-40 percent of American adults now own a smartwatch, indicating the category has moved from niche gadget to mass-market consumer device.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: At this penetration level, smartwatch health-data quality becomes a public-health and liability issue, not just a product-review footnote — relevant to any company positioning wearables as clinical-grade monitors.
insights.quote: roughly 30-40 percent of American adults own one of them

insights.claim: Smartwatches are increasingly marketed as monitors of clinical-style health metrics such as blood pressure and sweat loss, beyond their original role as timepieces and notification screens.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The expansion into quasi-medical claims raises the regulatory and reputational stakes for wearable makers if accuracy doesn't hold up.

insights.claim: Kinesiologists at the University of Michigan have developed a new framework to help consumers understand exactly what smartwatches are and are not measuring accurately.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A validated academic framework for grading wearable metric accuracy could become a reference point for regulators or reviewers evaluating health-tech marketing claims.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Kinesiologists from the University of Michigan"
